newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Traffic light kit gives go-ahead to lovers.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Traffic light kit gives go-ahead to lovers.

text.p: A revolutionary traffic light system which tells couples when they can make love without the risk of pregnancy could make major inroads in the market for condoms and the pill, its makers claimed on Monday.
Unipath, part of Anglo-Dutch consumer giant Unilever, said its new Persona monitoring kit will tell women exactly when they risk getting pregnant, by testing the hormones contained in urine.
"The monitor will indicate a green light when a woman is free to make love without using a contraceptive and a red light on the days on which she is at risk of becoming pregnant," Unipath said.
The company claimed 95 percent reliability for the kit, about the same as for condoms but below the 99 to 100 percent security offered by the pill.
The 49.95 pounds ($77.95) starter kit consists of a small hand-held monitor and 16 test sticks, which are used to build up a picture of a woman's individual cycle in the first month of use.
From then on it asks for only eight tests a month, with a yellow warning light showing when a test is needed. A month's supply of test kits will cost 9.95 pounds.
Unipath said there were millions of women dissatisfied with their choice in contraception and said it anticipated that many of them will adopt Persona as their new method.
British women will be the first to try the kit, which scientists have developed from Unipath's home fertility and pregnancy-testing kits Clearblue and Clearplan.

Franca Tranza, a spokeswoman for the family planning agency Marie Stopes International, welcomed the development as widening the choices open to women. But she added "it does not mean it will be suitable for everybody. If people are happy with the contraceptive they are using there is no reason to change."
Tranza said Persona will be most attractive to women concerned about side-effects from taking the pill, but warned that "if you opt for that you will be changing to a less secure method."

The leading suppliers of the contraceptive pill and condoms in Britain, respectively Schering Healthcare of Germany and London International Group Plc, greeted news of the breakthrough with equanimity.
A spokeswoman for LIG, the world's largest maker of condoms including the Durex brand, said any new innovation was welcome "because it raises general awareness..."
But she added "this is not a contraceptive in itself, and of course it doesn't protect against sexually-transmitted diseases."
Unipath said chemists chain Boots Co Plc will be offering information and advice to women who are interested in finding out more about the kit.

Carole Graham of Schering Healthcare, part of Schering AG, pointed to a survey on women's preferences published last week which showed that "the pill is far and away the most popular form of contraception in the U.K, despite scares and panics."
She said the survey showed that women "want something that won't affect spontaneity."
